newsitem.title: USA: Death penalty sought for 1995 New York City murder.
newsitem.headline: Death penalty sought for 1995 New York City murder.

text.p: A Kentucky man accused of murdering his gay lover will be the first defendant to face a possible death penalty in New York City since the state reintroduced capital punishment, officials said Tuesday.
"This was a most difficult decision. There is no glory in being first," said Brooklyn District Attorney Charles Hynes, who is personally opposed to capital punishment.

The accused man, Michael Shane Hale, 24, of Lexington, Kentucky, is charged with first-degree murder. He is accused of hacking to death his gay lover, Stefen Tanner, on Oct. 14, 1995, after a dispute over purchases he made with Tanner's credit card.

The indictment alleges that Hale hit his victim on the head several times and then drove the body in the trunk of the dead man's car to Kentucky, where he cut up the corpse with a hacksaw and dumped the parts into several trash cans.
Hynes said he will prosecute the case himself. "I cannot ask an assistant to try a capital case unless I'm willing to do it," he said.
Angel Diaz, accused of shooting a New York City police officer, was considered likely to be the first capital case in New York City, but he committed suicide this month in his jail cell.

Capital punishment was reinstated in New York state last year with the support of Republican Gov. George Pataki. His predecessor, Mario Cuomo, opposed the death penalty and vetoed capital punishement legislation consistently during his 12 years in office.
The death penalty is being sought in several cases elsewhere in New York state.
